guidance: A grid lookup, not a measurement: the page snaps the reading to the nearest ITU channel and reports the offset. Wavelengths are vacuum values, and a laser's real centre wavelength normally sits somewhere inside its tolerance band.
method: The dense plan is defined in frequency, not wavelength. ITU-T G.694.1 anchors the DWDM grid at 193.10 THz and spaces channels by 12.5, 25, 50 or 100 GHz from that anchor; this page implements the 100 GHz and 50 GHz plans, so the channel index n is the nearest whole number to (f minus 193.10 THz) divided by 0.1 or 0.05 THz, and the channel frequency is 193.10 THz plus n times the spacing. A negative n is a channel below the anchor, which is a longer wavelength: n = 0 is 1552.52 nm, n = +3 is 193.40 THz at 1550.12 nm, and n = -14 is 191.70 THz at 1563.86 nm. The wavelength follows from the frequency in vacuum, wavelength in nanometres equals 299,792.458 divided by the frequency in terahertz, because a nanometre times a terahertz is a thousand metres per second and the speed of light is 299,792,458 m/s. The coarse plan comes from ITU-T G.694.2: eighteen channels from 1271 to 1611 nm in 20 nm steps, so the channel number is the nearest whole number to (wavelength minus 1271) divided by 20, plus one, and channel 15 is 1551 nm at 193.2898 THz. Each result is labelled with its ITU band using the usual letter ranges, O 1260 to 1360, E 1360 to 1460, S 1460 to 1530, C 1530 to 1565, L 1565 to 1625 and U 1625 to 1675 nm, taking the lower edge as inclusive. Input is clamped to the range the plans cover: 186 to 200 THz, about 1612 to 1499 nm, for the DWDM grids, and 1271 to 1611 nm for CWDM; anything outside is refused rather than rounded into a channel the plan does not define. A value between channels is snapped to the nearest one and the offset is printed both in gigahertz and in nanometres, with offsets under 0.05 GHz treated as on grid because the display resolves 0.1 GHz. Frequencies print to four decimals of a terahertz and wavelengths to two decimals of a nanometre. The page reports the nearest channel only: it does not know a laser's tuning range, does not convert to the wavelength inside glass, which is shorter by the fiber's group index, and does not compute dispersion, optical signal-to-noise ratio or channel power. Everything runs in the browser.
